beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Most Hibernate problems come from a few causes: unbounded object graphs, queries generated without review, long transactions and schema drift. Good practice is to make each of them visible: log SQL in development, assert statement counts in tests, set timeouts, and manage the schema with migrations.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

A checklist: LAZY everywhere, fetch plans per use case (entity graph, join fetch, projection), SEQUENCE ids with batching, Set-based many-to-many, @Version on aggregates, EnumType.STRING, DTOs at the API, Flyway/Liquibase for schema, HikariCP sizing, and slow-query logging.

intermediate.content:
Avoiding N+1 Problem

N+1 problem occurs when lazy-loaded associations are fetched repeatedly, causing many SQL queries. Solve it using JOIN FETCH or entity graphs:

Batch Processing

For bulk inserts/updates, use batching to reduce database round-trips:

Performance Tuning

Improve Hibernate performance with:

  • Use LAZY fetching for collections
  • Enable second-level cache for frequently accessed entities
  • Use projections instead of fetching full entities when only some columns are needed
  • Use batch fetching and pagination for large datasets

expert.content:
Error Handling

Always handle exceptions properly to maintain data integrity and consistent application state:

Advanced Tips

  • Prefer HQL or Criteria API over native SQL for database independence.
  • Use @BatchSize or Hibernate-specific annotations to optimize collection fetching.
  • Monitor SQL generated by Hibernate to spot inefficient queries.
  • Use stateless sessions for very large batch operations without first-level caching overhead.
  • Consider read-only sessions for reporting queries to improve performance.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use @Version for concurrency, SEQUENCE ids with batching, and EnumType.STRING.
  • Avoid bidirectional relations unless needed, and keep them in sync with helper methods.
  • Do not expose entities in REST APIs; map to DTOs.

Senior Notes

  • Add query-count assertions to integration tests and enable statistics in staging.
  • Pool connections with HikariCP sized for the database and monitor pool wait time.
  • Use read-only transactions for queries, and move heavy analytics to SQL or a read model.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: update ddl-auto in production, exposing entities from controllers (lazy errors, over-posting), saving inside loops without batching, ignoring the SQL, and giant @Transactional methods that call remote services. Fix each with its counterpart.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Pool and database sizing: a small HikariCP pool outperforms a large one. Watch pool wait time, active connections, and statement counts per endpoint, and load test before changing settings.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world review checklist for a pull request touching persistence: new queries have indexes, statement count assertions exist, migrations are included, DTOs are used, transactions are on services, and no entity crosses the API boundary.

topics.name: Hibernate Architecture

beginner.content:
How Hibernate Sits Above JDBC

Hibernate doesn't replace JDBC - it sits on top of it, generating and executing JDBC calls on your behalf so you write Java objects and method calls instead of raw SQL strings and ResultSet loops.

     Your Application
            |
    Configuration  ---reads--->  hibernate.cfg.xml / properties
            |
      SessionFactory   (heavyweight, built ONCE, thread-safe)
            |
         Session       (lightweight, one per unit of work, NOT thread-safe)
            |
    +-------+--------+
    |                |
Transaction   Query / Criteria
    |                |
    +-------+--------+
            |
        JDBC Driver
            |
         Database

The Core Objects and What Each One Does

• Configuration - reads hibernate.cfg.xml (or properties) and your annotated entity classes, then builds a SessionFactory.
• SessionFactory - expensive to create, built once per application (or once per database), thread-safe, and shared everywhere. Think of it as a connection-pool-aware factory for Session objects.
• Session - a lightweight, single-threaded "unit of work" wrapping one JDBC connection. You open one, do some work, and close it - never share a Session across threads.
• Transaction - represents one atomic unit of work committed or rolled back together; every write should happen inside one.
• Query / Criteria - the objects you get back from session.createQuery(...) / session.createCriteria(...) to actually run HQL or programmatic queries.

Fresher Notes

  • Main parts: Configuration, SessionFactory, Session, Transaction, Query, and the persistence context.
  • SessionFactory is created once; Session is short-lived and not thread-safe.
  • Hibernate sits between your code and JDBC, translating objects to SQL.

Worked Example 1

Entity listener for auditing.

Worked Example 2

Second-level cache config.

Practice Exercise 1

Session per unit of work.

Practice Exercise 2

Flush behaviour.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Hibernate has layers: the API (Session, Query, Transaction), the core engine (persistence context, action queue, event listeners, loaders and persisters), the SQL generation layer (dialect, SQL AST) and JDBC services (connection provider, statement batching). An operation raises an event; default listeners update the persistence context and queue actions; flush turns actions into JDBC statements.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Extension points: event listeners (PreInsertEventListener), interceptors, custom types and converters, custom id generators, multi-tenancy resolvers (CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver), integrators and statistics. Flush modes control when SQL is sent: AUTO, COMMIT, ALWAYS, MANUAL.

expert.content:
Primary Key Generation Strategies: GenerationType Compared

@GeneratedValue(strategy = ...) controls HOW the primary key value is produced, and the 4 strategies behave very differently under the hood:
StrategyHow it worksNotes
IDENTITYDelegates to the DB's auto-increment columnSimple, but disables Hibernate's JDBC batching for inserts (id isn't known until after the INSERT)
SEQUENCEUses a database sequence object to pre-fetch id valuesBatching-friendly; only supported by DBs with sequences (Oracle, PostgreSQL - MySQL has no native sequence)
TABLEUses a separate table to simulate a sequenceWorks on any database, but slowest - needs its own row-level locking
AUTOHibernate picks a strategy based on the configured dialectConvenient default, but less predictable/portable than choosing explicitly

@Column Attributes Beyond the Name

@Column does more than rename a field - it also constrains the generated DDL and validation:
• nullable = false - generates a NOT NULL constraint.
• length = 100 - sets a VARCHAR length (defaults to 255).
• unique = true - adds a unique constraint on that column.
• updatable = false / insertable = false - excludes the field from UPDATE/INSERT statements (useful for computed or DB-managed columns).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why is SessionFactory built only once but Session opened per request?SessionFactory is thread-safe and expensive to construct (parses config/mappings); Session is cheap, single-threaded, and scoped to one unit of work
Why does IDENTITY disable batch inserts?Hibernate needs the generated id immediately after each INSERT to keep the persistence context consistent, forcing one round-trip per row instead of batching
Which GenerationType works identically across all databases?TABLE - it simulates a sequence using an ordinary table, at the cost of extra locking overhead
What does @Column(updatable = false) do?Excludes that field from any generated UPDATE statement, even if the field's value changes in Java - useful for created_at timestamps
Is a Session thread-safe?No - a Session is single-threaded and must never be shared across threads, unlike the thread-safe SessionFactory

Mid-Level Notes

  • Flow: the application calls Session methods; Hibernate keeps entities in the persistence context; at flush it generates SQL via the dialect; JDBC executes it over a pooled connection.
  • Caches: first-level (Session) and optional second-level and query caches.
  • Interceptors and event listeners allow hooks (auditing, multi-tenancy).

Senior Notes

  • Understand flush modes (AUTO flushes before queries that might be affected) and why unexpected SQL appears before a query.
  • Multi-tenancy (schema or discriminator) and filters are supported through resolvers and @Filter.
  • Know the bootstrap process (metadata, integrators, JDBC services) when debugging startup or custom integrations.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: sharing a Session across threads, long-lived sessions (stale and large persistence context), unexpected flushes before queries (AUTO), and mutating entities by accident in read paths. Use short sessions, read-only mode where possible and be aware of flush ordering.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Memory and CPU: each managed entity keeps a snapshot for dirty checking, so loading 100,000 entities doubles the memory. For read-only work use projections or read-only queries; for bulk work use StatelessSession.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: multi-tenant application. A resolver supplies the tenant id for each request, Hibernate selects the schema or adds a discriminator filter, and the same code serves all tenants.

topics.name: Introduction, ORM and Comparisons: JDBC, JPA, Spring Data JPA

beginner.content:
What is Hibernate and what is ORM?

• Hibernate ORM is an open-source Java framework that maps Java objects to relational tables (Object-Relational Mapping) and generates the SQL for you. You work with entities and a session/entity manager; Hibernate issues INSERT/SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE, manages connections, and keeps objects and rows in sync.
• ORM bridges the object-relational impedance mismatch: objects have inheritance, references and identity, tables have rows, foreign keys and keys. Hibernate handles type conversion, associations, inheritance mapping, caching, lazy loading and dirty checking.
• Hibernate is the most widely used JPA implementation and is the default provider in Spring Boot.

intermediate.content:
Hibernate vs JDBC vs JPA vs Spring Data JPA

JDBCHibernate (native API)JPASpring Data JPA
What it isLow-level database APIORM frameworkSpecification (Jakarta Persistence)Repository abstraction on top of JPA
SQLYou write all of itGenerated + HQL/nativeGenerated + JPQL/nativeDerived from method names, @Query
MappingManual (ResultSet)Annotations/XMLAnnotationsEntities (JPA)
PortabilitySQL dialect specificHibernate-specific extrasProvider independentJPA + Spring
BoilerplateHighLowLowLowest
ControlTotalHighHighConvenient, can hide SQL
• JPA defines the API (EntityManager, annotations, JPQL); Hibernate implements it (and adds extras: Session, HQL features, filters, @BatchSize); Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations and integrates with Spring transactions. Hibernate uses JDBC underneath, so JDBC knowledge still matters (batching, pooling, transactions).

expert.content:
When to use what

• Spring Data JPA + Hibernate: the default for CRUD-heavy business applications and microservices: fast to build, readable, good productivity.
• JDBC / JdbcTemplate / jOOQ for reporting, bulk loads, complex SQL, or hot paths where you need exact SQL control; mixing both in one service is normal.
• Know the cost of ORM: hidden SQL, N+1 queries, memory use of large persistence contexts, the learning curve of lifecycle and lazy loading. Mitigate by reading the SQL log, using DTO projections for read models and keeping transactions short.
• Hibernate-specific features (filters, @Formula, @NaturalId, @BatchSize, @SoftDelete) trade portability for power: acceptable, but isolate them.

interviewQA: What is Hibernate?

An open-source ORM framework for Java that maps entity classes to database tables, generates SQL, manages persistence context, caching, lazy loading and transactions, and is the most widely used implementation of the JPA specification.
Hibernate vs JPA?

JPA is a specification (the jakarta.persistence API); Hibernate is an implementation of it with extra native features (Session, HQL extensions, filters). Code written to JPA can switch providers; Hibernate-specific APIs cannot.
Hibernate vs JDBC?

JDBC is a low-level API where you write SQL and map ResultSets yourself. Hibernate builds on JDBC and automates mapping, SQL generation, caching, dirty checking and associations, reducing boilerplate at the cost of some control.

topics.name: Architecture, Configuration, Dependencies, Annotations and SessionFactory

beginner.content:
Hibernate architecture

• Your application talks to the persistence API (EntityManager/Session). Core objects: SessionFactory (heavyweight, thread-safe, one per database, built once at startup; holds metadata, SQL cache, second-level cache config), Session (lightweight, not thread-safe, one unit of work, wraps a JDBC connection and holds the persistence context = first-level cache), Transaction, and query objects.
• Below sit the mapping metadata (annotations), the dialect (database-specific SQL), the connection provider (pool) and JDBC. Hibernate translates entity operations into SQL, executes through JDBC and maps results back to objects.

intermediate.content:
Dependencies and configuration

• Spring Boot (recommended): add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa (brings Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, HikariCP) and a JDBC driver; configure in application.properties. The auto-configured EntityManagerFactory is a Hibernate SessionFactory.
• Plain Hibernate: org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core + driver + a connection pool; configure with hibernate.cfg.xml, persistence.xml or a Configuration object.
• Key properties: hibernate.dialect (auto-detected in Hibernate 6), hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto (validate in production, never create/update), hibernate.show_sql, hibernate.format_sql, hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size.
codeExamples:
<!-- pom.xml -->
<dependency><groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>com.mysql</groupId><artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId><scope>runtime</scope></dependency>
<!-- or PostgreSQL: org.postgresql:postgresql -->

# application.properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/javaschoollab
spring.datasource.username=jsl
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate                  # schema comes from Flyway; Hibernate only checks it
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false                           # do not keep the session open during view rendering
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=32
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE         # show bind parameters

expert.content:
Annotations overview and SessionFactory vs EntityManagerFactory

GroupAnnotations
Entity and table@Entity, @Table, @Id, @GeneratedValue, @Column, @Transient, @Enumerated, @Lob, @Embedded/@Embeddable
Relationships@OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany, @JoinColumn, @JoinTable
Inheritance@Inheritance, @DiscriminatorColumn, @MappedSuperclass
Locking and audit@Version, @PrePersist/@PreUpdate, @EntityListeners
Hibernate-specific@BatchSize, @Fetch, @Cache, @Filter, @Formula, @NaturalId, @DynamicUpdate, @SoftDelete, @CreationTimestamp
• SessionFactory (Hibernate) and EntityManagerFactory (JPA) are the same object: SessionFactory extends EntityManagerFactory. Create it once; it is expensive and thread-safe. Unwrap when you need Hibernate features: emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class), em.unwrap(Session.class).

interviewQA: What is the SessionFactory and why is it created once?

A thread-safe, heavyweight factory that holds mapping metadata, the dialect, connection and cache configuration and creates Sessions. Building it is expensive, so an application creates one per database at startup.
SessionFactory vs EntityManagerFactory?
They are the same thing: SessionFactory extends the JPA EntityManagerFactory with Hibernate-specific features. In Spring Boot the EntityManagerFactory bean is a SessionFactory you can unwrap.
Why set ddl-auto to validate in production?
create/update can change or drop schema automatically and are unsafe. validate only checks that entities match the schema, which should be managed by migration tools such as Flyway or Liquibase.

topics.name: Entity Classes and Mapping: @Entity, @Table, @Id, @Column, @Transient, @Enumerated, java.time

beginner.content:
A basic entity

• An entity is a class mapped to a table. Requirements: annotated @Entity, an @Id field, a no-argument constructor (at least protected), not final (Hibernate creates proxy subclasses), non-final persistent fields/methods.
• @Table(name, schema, uniqueConstraints, indexes) sets the table; @Column(name, nullable, length, unique, precision, scale, updatable, insertable, columnDefinition) customises a column. Without annotations, a field maps to a column of the same name (Spring Boot's naming strategy converts camelCase to snake_case).

intermediate.content:
@Enumerated, @Transient, date/time and LOBs

• @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) is safe: the default ORDINAL stores 0,1,2 and breaks when you reorder or insert enum constants. (Hibernate 6 can also map enums to native database enum types.)
• @Transient (or Java's transient) excludes a field from persistence: derived or UI-only values.
• @Temporal is legacy, needed only for java.util.Date/Calendar (TemporalType.DATE|TIME|TIMESTAMP). For new code use java.time types, which Hibernate maps natively: LocalDate → DATE, LocalTime → TIME, LocalDateTime → TIMESTAMP, Instant/OffsetDateTime/ZonedDateTime → TIMESTAMP (WITH TIME ZONE). Store UTC instants for events and a LocalDate for birthdays.
• @Lob for large text/binary (String → CLOB, byte[] → BLOB); avoid loading large LOBs unnecessarily (@Basic(fetch = LAZY) needs bytecode enhancement).

expert.content:
Embedded types, naming and equality

• @Embeddable / @Embedded map a value object into columns of the owning table (no separate table or identity): Address, Money, AuditFields. Reuse with @AttributeOverrides. Embeddables make the model expressive and avoid wide classes.
• Naming: Spring Boot uses CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy and PhysicalNamingStrategy; set explicit names for shared schemas.
• Equality: do not use all fields. Implement equals/hashCode on a business key (@NaturalId) or on the id with null handling and a constant hashCode per class; never use lazy collections in them. Lombok @Data on entities is a classic bug source (toString/equals traverse lazy associations).
• Prefer immutability where possible (@Immutable for read-only reference tables).

interviewQA: Why use EnumType.STRING instead of ORDINAL?
ORDINAL stores the position (0, 1, 2), so reordering or inserting constants silently corrupts existing data. STRING stores the constant name, which is stable and readable.
Is @Temporal still needed?
Only for legacy java.util.Date and Calendar. With java.time types (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Instant, OffsetDateTime) Hibernate maps date/time natively without @Temporal.
Why must an entity have a no-arg constructor and not be final?
Hibernate instantiates entities reflectively and creates runtime proxy subclasses for lazy loading; a final class or missing constructor prevents proxying and instantiation.

topics.name: Primary Keys and @GeneratedValue Strategies

beginner.content:
Choosing an identifier

• @Id marks the primary key. Types: Long (most common), Integer, UUID, String (natural keys), embedded/composite keys. Use wrapper types (Long, not long) so a transient entity has id == null.
• @GeneratedValue(strategy) lets the database or Hibernate generate it: IDENTITY (auto-increment column), SEQUENCE (database sequence, with a generator), TABLE (rarely), AUTO (provider picks: sequence on PostgreSQL/Oracle, identity or sequence emulation on MySQL), and UUID (Hibernate 6: GenerationType.UUID).

intermediate.content:
Strategy trade-offs

StrategyHowProsCons
IDENTITYDB auto-incrementSimple, human-friendly idsInsert executes at persist() to learn the id; no JDBC batch inserts
SEQUENCEDB sequence, pooled optimiserBatch-friendly, id known before flush, fewer round tripsNot on MySQL < 8 (emulated with a table); need allocationSize = sequence INCREMENT BY
UUID128-bit random/time-basedUnique across services/DBs, no coordination, no id enumerationLarger index, random UUIDs fragment B-trees (prefer time-ordered)
TABLERow in a tablePortableSlow, lock contention: avoid
AUTOProvider decidesConvenientBehaviour differs per database: be explicit
• Rule: PostgreSQL/Oracle → SEQUENCE with allocationSize matching the sequence INCREMENT BY; MySQL → IDENTITY (accept no batching for inserts) or UUID; microservices that publish ids across services often prefer UUIDs.

expert.content:
Sequence tuning, pooled optimisers and key design

• Pooled optimiser (the default for SEQUENCE in Hibernate 6): one sequence call reserves allocationSize ids; allocationSize = 50 means 50 inserts per round trip to the sequence. If several application instances share the sequence, the pooled optimiser still avoids collisions because the sequence increments by the same size.
• Do not expose database ids in URLs if enumeration matters: use a public UUID or @NaturalId slug alongside the surrogate key. Natural keys (email, ISBN) change more often than expected: prefer surrogate primary keys with a unique constraint on the natural key.
• Testing id generation: the first persisted entity per transaction shows whether ids come from a sequence call (select nextval) or the insert itself; check the SQL log. Changing the strategy of a live table needs a migration (sequence start value must be above the current max id).

interviewQA: Why does IDENTITY disable JDBC batch inserts?
Hibernate must execute each INSERT immediately to obtain the generated key, so it cannot queue and batch inserts. SEQUENCE ids can be allocated up front, so inserts can be batched.
What is allocationSize in @SequenceGenerator?
The number of ids Hibernate reserves from the sequence per call (pooled optimiser). It must match the sequence INCREMENT BY, otherwise ids collide or are wasted.
When are UUID primary keys a good idea?
In distributed or microservice systems needing globally unique ids without coordination, or to avoid exposing guessable ids; use time-ordered UUIDs to limit index fragmentation.

topics.name: Entity Lifecycle, Persistence Context, Session vs EntityManager

beginner.content:
Entity states

• Transient (new): created with new, no id (or not associated), not in the database, unknown to Hibernate.
• Persistent (managed): associated with an open persistence context (Session/EntityManager). Hibernate tracks it: changes are detected (dirty checking) and written at flush/commit. Returned by find(), queries, and after persist().
• Detached: has a database identity but its persistence context was closed/cleared; changes are not tracked. Reattach with merge().
• Removed: scheduled for deletion at flush (remove()).
codeExamples:
Course c = new Course("JPA", "jpa", BigDecimal.TEN, Level.BEGINNER);   // TRANSIENT

em.getTransaction().begin();
em.persist(c);                          // -> PERSISTENT (insert at flush/commit, or immediately with IDENTITY)
c.setPrice(BigDecimal.valueOf(20));     // tracked: UPDATE at flush (dirty checking)
em.getTransaction().commit();           // flush + commit

em.detach(c);                           // -> DETACHED: further changes are ignored
c.setPrice(BigDecimal.valueOf(30));     // NOT saved

em.getTransaction().begin();
Course managed = em.merge(c);           // copies state onto a MANAGED instance and returns it (c itself stays detached)
em.remove(managed);                     // -> REMOVED: DELETE at flush
em.getTransaction().commit();

intermediate.content:
The persistence context (first-level cache)

• The persistence context is the set of managed entities of one EntityManager/Session: a first-level cache and identity map (one instance per row per context), a unit of work (change tracking) and the place where write-behind batching happens.
• Guarantees: find(Course.class, 1L) twice in the same context returns the same Java object and runs one SELECT; entities are flushed in a defined order (inserts, updates, collection changes, deletes).
• Lifetime: with Spring, a transaction-scoped persistence context starts and ends with the @Transactional method; entities returned from a service become detached after it returns. (Open Session In View extends it to the web request: disable it with spring.jpa.open-in-view=false.)

expert.content:
Session vs EntityManager

EntityManager (JPA)Session (Hibernate)
StandardJakarta PersistenceHibernate-specific; Session extends EntityManager
Savepersist(), merge()same, plus legacy save(), saveOrUpdate(), update() (removed in Hibernate 6.x)
Loadfind(), getReference()same, plus legacy get(), load(), plus byId(), byNaturalId(), byMultipleIds()
Extras—setDefaultReadOnly, setHibernateFlushMode, filters (enableFilter), doWork, stateless sessions, statistics
• In Spring Boot inject EntityManager via @PersistenceContext (a thread-safe shared proxy bound to the current transaction) and unwrap to Session only when you need Hibernate features. EntityManagerFactory/SessionFactory are the factories (see Fundamentals).

interviewQA: What are the entity states in Hibernate?
Transient (new, unknown to Hibernate), persistent/managed (attached to a persistence context and tracked), detached (has an id but its context closed) and removed (scheduled for deletion).
What is the persistence context?
The set of entities managed by one EntityManager/Session: a first-level cache and identity map, the change-tracking unit of work and the write-behind queue flushed to the database at commit.
Session vs EntityManager?

EntityManager is the JPA standard interface; Session is Hibernate's native interface that extends it with extra features (filters, stateless/read-only modes, byNaturalId, legacy methods). In Spring you normally inject EntityManager and unwrap Session when needed.

topics.name: Insert, Select, Update, Delete: persist, merge, remove, find, getReference

beginner.content:
Insert and select

• Insert: em.persist(entity) makes a transient entity managed and schedules an INSERT (executed at flush/commit, or immediately for IDENTITY). The id is available after persist for sequence/identity generators.
• Select by id: em.find(Class, id) hits the persistence context, then the database (SELECT), returns the entity or null. em.getReference(Class, id) returns a lazy proxy without a query (throws EntityNotFoundException on first access if missing): ideal for setting a foreign key without loading the row.
• Legacy Hibernate: session.get() ≈ find(); session.load() ≈ getReference().

intermediate.content:
Update and delete

• Update: load the entity (managed) and change it: dirty checking issues the UPDATE at flush; no save()/update() call is needed inside a transaction. For a detached entity use em.merge(entity), which loads the managed copy, copies state and returns the managed instance.
• Delete: em.remove(managedEntity) (must be managed; for a detached one use em.remove(em.merge(e)) or em.getReference). Cascades apply. Bulk delete/update with JPQL (delete from Course c where ...) bypasses the persistence context and lifecycle callbacks.
• Use @DynamicUpdate to include only changed columns in UPDATE statements (wide tables).

expert.content:
persist vs merge, and the legacy save/update

persist()merge()
InputTransient entityTransient or detached
ResultThe same instance becomes managedReturns a different managed copy; the argument stays unmanaged
SQLINSERT onlySELECT (to load by id) then INSERT or UPDATE
On a detached entityThrows PersistentObjectExceptionReattaches state
Cascade typePERSISTMERGE
• Legacy Hibernate: save() (insert, returns id), update() (reattach and update), saveOrUpdate(); they were deprecated and removed in Hibernate 6.x: use persist()/merge(). Spring Data's repository.save(entity) calls persist if the entity is new (isNew(): id null or @Version null) else merge.
• Gotcha: with assigned ids, save() thinks the entity is not new and performs a SELECT + merge: implement Persistable or use a @Version.

interviewQA: persist() vs merge()?

persist makes a transient instance managed and schedules an INSERT, keeping the same object; merge copies the state of a transient/detached instance onto a managed copy (loading by id) and returns that copy, issuing INSERT or UPDATE as needed.
find() vs getReference()?

find returns the entity (hitting the database if not in the persistence context) or null; getReference returns a lazy proxy without a query and throws EntityNotFoundException on first access if the row does not exist. Use getReference to set foreign keys cheaply.
Do you need to call save() to update a managed entity?
No. Changes to a managed entity are detected by dirty checking and written at flush/commit. save() is only needed for new or detached entities.

topics.name: flush(), clear(), refresh(), detach() and Legacy Operations

beginner.content:
flush() and clear()

• flush() synchronises the persistence context with the database: it executes pending INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements (inside the current transaction, not committed yet). It happens automatically before commit and (in FlushMode.AUTO) before a query that could be affected.
• clear() detaches all managed entities and empties the first-level cache without flushing: unflushed changes are lost. Typical use: batch processing: flush(); clear(); every N rows to keep memory flat.
• commit() = flush + commit of the database transaction (changes become durable and visible).

intermediate.content:
refresh() and detach()

• refresh(entity) re-reads the row and overwrites the entity's state (discarding unflushed changes): use after a database trigger/other transaction changed data or to undo changes. Cascades with CascadeType.REFRESH.
• detach(entity) removes one entity (and cascaded ones) from the persistence context: changes stop being tracked. Use for read-only copies or to avoid flushing an entity. em.contains(e) tells if it is managed.
• em.lock(entity, lockMode) and em.getFlushMode()/setFlushMode() complete the API.

expert.content:
Legacy Hibernate APIs and migration

Legacy (Session)Modern (JPA)Notes
save(e)persist(e)save returned the id and could be used on assigned ids; removed in Hibernate 6.x
update(e)merge(e)update reattached the given instance and always issued an UPDATE
saveOrUpdate(e)persist / mergeGuessing based on id: ambiguous
get(Class, id)find(Class, id)Same behaviour
load(Class, id)getReference(Class, id)Lazy proxy
delete(e)remove(e)—
createCriteria() (legacy)CriteriaBuilder (JPA)Removed in Hibernate 6
• When migrating old code, replace these APIs and re-test lifecycle behaviour (especially update() semantics on detached graphs).

interviewQA: flush() vs commit()?
flush sends pending SQL to the database inside the open transaction (not yet durable/visible to others); commit performs a flush and then commits the database transaction, making changes permanent.
What does clear() do and why use it in batch jobs?
It detaches all entities and empties the persistence context without flushing, releasing memory. In bulk imports flush() then clear() every N rows to avoid OutOfMemoryError and slow dirty checking.
refresh() vs find()?
find may return a cached managed instance without hitting the database; refresh always reloads the row and overwrites the managed entity state, discarding unflushed changes.

topics.name: Transaction Management in Hibernate and JPA

beginner.content:
Transactions with the persistence API

• All modifications must run inside a transaction. A transaction groups operations into an atomic unit: begin → work → commit (or rollback on failure).
• Resource-local (plain Hibernate/JPA on Java SE): em.getTransaction().begin()/commit()/rollback(). Container/Spring-managed: @Transactional (see Transactions section). JTA for distributed transactions across resources (rare in microservices).
• Always roll back on exception and close the EntityManager (try-with-resources / finally). Keep transactions short: do not call remote services or wait for user input while a transaction (and its database connection) is open.

intermediate.content:
Rollback rules and common mistakes

• JPA marks the transaction rollback-only when a runtime exception (including PersistenceException) occurs; you cannot continue and commit. In Spring, @Transactional rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default and commits on checked exceptions unless you set rollbackFor.
• Mistakes: swallowing an exception inside a transaction (then commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException), calling a @Transactional method from the same class (self-invocation bypasses the proxy), putting @Transactional on private/non-public methods, long transactions holding connections, and doing remote calls inside them.
• Read-only transactions (@Transactional(readOnly = true)) let Hibernate skip dirty checking and flushing (and Spring can route to read replicas).

expert.content:
Transaction boundaries in practice

• Define boundaries at the use case (service method), not around individual repository calls: each repository call without an outer transaction runs in its own transaction and persistence context, so two consecutive calls are not atomic and entities become detached between them.
• Read-then-write must be atomic: load and update in one transaction (and use @Version or locks to protect against concurrent changes).
• Avoid mixing remote calls (HTTP, messaging) with database changes in one transaction: if the remote call succeeds and the commit fails, they are inconsistent. Use the transactional outbox pattern: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction and publish it afterwards.
• Test rollbacks: @DataJpaTest rolls back each test by default; use @Commit or TestTransaction when you need to verify committed behaviour.

interviewQA: What happens to a JPA transaction when an exception occurs?

The transaction is marked rollback-only for persistence exceptions; commit will fail. In Spring, @Transactional rolls back for unchecked exceptions by default and commits for checked ones unless rollbackFor is specified.
Why keep transactions short?
An open transaction holds a database connection and locks; long ones exhaust the connection pool, increase lock contention and deadlock risk, so do remote calls and slow work outside them.
Why does @Transactional not work on a method called from the same class?
Spring applies it through a proxy; an internal call (this.method()) bypasses the proxy, so no transaction is started. Move the method to another bean or inject self.

topics.name: One-to-One, Many-to-One, One-to-Many, @JoinColumn and mappedBy

beginner.content:
@ManyToOne: the foundation

• @ManyToOne (many enrolments → one course) puts the foreign key column in the table of the "many" side: it is the owning side and the simplest, most efficient mapping. Use @JoinColumn(name = "course_id", nullable = false).
• Default fetch is EAGER for @ManyToOne/@OneToOne: set fetch = FetchType.LAZY explicitly almost always, to avoid loading extra rows and N+1 queries.
• Owning side = the side that has the foreign key and whose changes Hibernate persists; inverse side = the side with mappedBy (read-only mirror).

intermediate.content:
@OneToMany and bidirectional mappings

• @OneToMany(mappedBy = "course") on the "one" side makes the relationship bidirectional: Course.enrollments is the inverse side (no extra columns; the FK is owned by Enrollment.course). Always prefer this over a unidirectional @OneToMany with @JoinColumn/join table (extra UPDATE statements or an extra table).
• Keep both sides in sync with helper methods (addEnrollment/removeEnrollment) that set both references; otherwise the in-memory graph is inconsistent and only the owning side is persisted.
• Initialise collections (new ArrayList<>() / LinkedHashSet), expose them unmodifiable, and use cascade/orphanRemoval for parent-owned children (an order and its lines), not for independent entities.

expert.content:
@OneToOne and owning vs inverse side

• @OneToOne: a student has one profile. Best mapping: shared primary key with @MapsId (the child's PK is also its FK), or a unique FK column with @JoinColumn(unique = true). Mark the owning side fetch = LAZY. The inverse side (mappedBy) of a one-to-one is always loaded eagerly in practice (Hibernate must query to know whether it is null) unless you use bytecode enhancement, optional=false is not enough: model it from the owning side if possible, or query by FK.
• Rules of thumb: owning side = side with the foreign key; only the owning side's state is persisted; the inverse side exists for navigation. Choose unidirectional from the many side whenever you can.

interviewQA: What are the owning and inverse sides?
The owning side has the foreign key and its state is what Hibernate persists; the inverse side (mappedBy) is a read-only mirror used for navigation. Changes made only on the inverse side are ignored.
What does mappedBy mean?
It states that the relationship is mapped by a field on the other entity (the owning side), so this side adds no column or join table of its own.
Why should @ManyToOne be set to LAZY?
The JPA default for @ManyToOne and @OneToOne is EAGER, which loads the associated row immediately and causes extra queries and N+1 problems. Declare fetch = LAZY and fetch what you need explicitly.

topics.name: Many-to-Many, @JoinTable, Bidirectional vs Unidirectional

beginner.content:
@ManyToMany with @JoinTable

• @ManyToMany models students ↔ courses with a join (link) table holding two foreign keys. The owning side declares @JoinTable(name, joinColumns, inverseJoinColumns); the other side uses mappedBy.
• Use a Set (not List) for many-to-many collections: with a List (a "bag") Hibernate deletes all link rows and re-inserts them on any change. Never use CascadeType.REMOVE/ALL on many-to-many (deleting one entity would delete shared ones).
• Keep both sides in sync with helper methods and implement equals/hashCode on a business key so Set semantics work.

intermediate.content:
When the link has data: use an association entity

• As soon as the relationship has its own attributes (enrolled date, grade, status) a plain @ManyToMany cannot hold them. Model the link table as an entity with two @ManyToOne associations (and optionally a composite or surrogate key). This is also the better default for most real many-to-many relationships: it is queryable, extensible and avoids bag/set surprises.
• Then the "many-to-many" becomes two one-to-many relationships: Student 1-* Enrollment *-1 Course.

expert.content:
Unidirectional vs bidirectional: choosing

UnidirectionalBidirectional
NavigationOne direction (Enrollment → Course)Both directions
ComplexitySimple; fewer sync bugsNeeds helper methods, mappedBy, careful toString/equals
QueriesQuery from the owning sideConvenient graph traversal
RecommendedDefault choice: @ManyToOne onlyOnly when you really navigate from the "one" side (parent-owned children with cascade)
• Bidirectional pitfalls: infinite recursion in toString, Jackson serialisation (@JsonIgnore/DTOs/@JsonManagedReference), forgetting to set both sides, lazy collections triggering SELECTs, equals/hashCode using collections. Do not expose entities from REST controllers: map to DTOs.
• Unidirectional @OneToMany (parent has a list, child has no back reference) without mappedBy produces an extra join table or extra UPDATEs: avoid it, or use @OneToMany @JoinColumn(name="course_id") knowingly.

interviewQA: Why use a Set instead of a List in @ManyToMany?
A List (bag) has no identity, so Hibernate deletes all rows of the link table and re-inserts them when the collection changes; a Set lets it delete and insert only the affected rows.
When should a many-to-many become an entity?
When the relationship has its own attributes (date, status, grade) or needs to be queried or audited: model the link table as an entity with two @ManyToOne associations.
How do you handle bidirectional relationships safely?

Maintain both sides with helper methods, make one side the owner (the one with the FK) and the other mappedBy, avoid entities in toString/equals that touch lazy collections, and return DTOs rather than entities from controllers.

topics.name: Cascade Types, Orphan Removal and Fetch Types (Lazy vs Eager)

beginner.content:
Cascade types

• Cascading propagates an operation from a parent to its associated entities. CascadeType: PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH, ALL (all of them), plus Hibernate's @Cascade(SAVE_UPDATE...) (legacy).
• Use cascade for composition (the child cannot exist without the parent: order → order lines, course → lessons). Do not cascade to independent aggregates (course → category, student → country) and never REMOVE/ALL on @ManyToMany or @ManyToOne.
• Cascading REMOVE loads the children and issues one DELETE per child (slow for large collections): consider @OnDelete(action = OnDeleteAction.CASCADE) (database ON DELETE CASCADE) or a bulk delete.

intermediate.content:
Orphan removal

• orphanRemoval = true deletes a child row when it is removed from the parent's collection (or its reference is set to null for one-to-one). It models "this child belongs to exactly one parent". It is stronger than CascadeType.REMOVE, which only deletes children when the parent is deleted.
• Use only on @OneToMany/@OneToOne where the child is exclusively owned. Do not replace the collection instance (setLines(newList)): Hibernate loses track and throws "A collection with cascade=all-delete-orphan was no longer referenced": mutate the existing collection (clear() + addAll()).

expert.content:
Fetch types: LAZY vs EAGER

• LAZY: the association is loaded on first access (via a proxy for to-one, a PersistentBag/Set for collections), needing an open session. EAGER: loaded together with the owner (a join or follow-up SELECT), always.
AssociationJPA defaultRecommendation
@ManyToOne, @OneToOneEAGERSet LAZY
@OneToMany, @ManyToManyLAZYKeep LAZY
@ElementCollectionLAZYKeep LAZY
• EAGER is a design smell: it cannot be switched off per query, multiplies queries (N+1) and loads data you do not need. Make everything LAZY in the mapping and fetch what a use case needs explicitly (join fetch, entity graphs, projections).
• LazyInitializationException: accessing a lazy association after the session closed. Fix by fetching in the query/transaction, using DTOs, or entity graphs; not by switching to EAGER or enabling Open Session In View.

interviewQA: What is cascading and which types exist?
Cascading propagates entity operations from a parent to its associations: PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH, or ALL. Use it for composition (order lines), not for independent entities.
Cascade REMOVE vs orphanRemoval?

REMOVE deletes children when the parent is deleted; orphanRemoval also deletes a child when it is removed from the parent's collection (or the reference is nulled), even though the parent still exists.
Lazy vs eager loading and how do you fix LazyInitializationException?

Lazy loads an association on first access (needs an open session); eager loads it with the owner. Fix the exception by fetching required data inside the transaction (join fetch, entity graph, DTO projection), not by making everything eager.

topics.name: HQL, JPQL, Native SQL and Parameterized Queries

beginner.content:
JPQL and HQL

• JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language) is the standard object-oriented query language: you query entities and their fields, not tables and columns. HQL is Hibernate's superset (more functions, from Course without select, extra joins). In Hibernate 6 both are processed by the same engine (SQM).
• Create with em.createQuery(jpql, ResultType.class) (typed): getResultList(), getSingleResult() (throws if none/many), getResultStream(), executeUpdate() for bulk update/delete.
• Entity names are case-sensitive, keywords are not. Navigate associations with dot notation (c.category.name) which generates implicit joins.

intermediate.content:
Parameterized queries and SQL injection

• Always bind parameters: named (:name, preferred) or positional (?1). Parameters are sent to the database as bind variables (JDBC PreparedStatement): prevents SQL injection, enables statement caching and plan reuse, and handles quoting/types.
• Never concatenate user input into a query string. For a dynamic order by use a whitelist of allowed fields; for dynamic where use Criteria/Specifications.
• like with wildcards: build the pattern in Java and bind it ("%" + escape(q) + "%"), or use concat/lower in the query.

expert.content:
Native SQL queries

• em.createNativeQuery(sql, Entity.class) executes database-specific SQL and maps columns to an entity, a @SqlResultSetMapping (DTO), or an Object[]/Tuple. Use for features JPQL lacks: window functions, recursive CTEs, database functions, hints, full-text search, complex reports, upserts.
• Trade-offs: not portable, no entity name abstraction, results bypass the persistence context unless mapped to entities. Flush before native queries (Hibernate flushes automatically only if it knows the affected tables: pass query spaces or call flush()).
• In Spring Data JPA: @Query(value = "...", nativeQuery = true); for pagination add a countQuery.

interviewQA: JPQL vs HQL vs native SQL?
JPQL is the standard entity-based query language; HQL is Hibernate's superset of it; native SQL is database-specific SQL on tables and columns, useful for features JPQL lacks but not portable.
Why use parameterised queries?
Parameters are sent as bind variables, preventing SQL injection, enabling statement and plan caching and handling types/quoting correctly. Never concatenate user input into queries.
When would you use a native query?
For database-specific features (window functions, recursive CTEs, full-text search, upserts) and complex reporting queries that are awkward in JPQL, accepting reduced portability.

topics.name: Criteria API and Named Queries

beginner.content:
Criteria API

• The Criteria API builds queries programmatically and type-safely: CriteriaBuilder → CriteriaQuery<T> → Root<E> → Predicates. Best for dynamic queries (search forms with optional filters) where string concatenation would be error-prone.
• It is verbose; combine with the JPA static metamodel (Course_.title, generated by hibernate-jpamodelgen) for compile-time safety. Spring Data's Specifications wrap it nicely. (The old session.createCriteria() is removed in Hibernate 6.)

intermediate.content:
Criteria with joins, aggregates and tuples

• root.join("category")/fetch(...) (join fetch), cb.count, cb.sum, cb.avg, groupBy, having, subqueries (cq.subquery(...)), cb.construct(Dto.class, ...) for DTO projections, CriteriaQuery<Tuple> with multiselect.
• Hibernate 6 also offers CriteriaDefinition/HibernateCriteriaBuilder with more functions.

expert.content:
Named queries

• A named query is a JPQL/native query with a name, declared on the entity (@NamedQuery, @NamedNativeQuery) and validated at startup (syntax errors appear at boot, not at first use) and pre-parsed. Create with em.createNamedQuery("Course.byLevel", Course.class).
• Good for stable, reused queries; clutters entities, so many teams prefer repository @Query methods (Spring Data registers them as named queries under the hood) or external META-INF/orm.xml. Naming convention: Entity.queryName.

interviewQA: When is the Criteria API better than JPQL?

For dynamic queries with optional filters, where building JPQL by string concatenation is error-prone; Criteria (or Spring Data Specifications) composes predicates safely and type-checks them with the metamodel.
What are the benefits of named queries?
They are validated and parsed at startup, reusable by name and keep queries separate from code; mistakes are caught at boot rather than at runtime.
What is the JPA static metamodel?
Generated classes such as Course_ with typed attribute references (Course_.title) used in Criteria queries for compile-time safety instead of string attribute names.

topics.name: Pagination, Sorting, Aggregates, Joins, Subqueries, Projections and DTO Projections

beginner.content:
Pagination and sorting

• Offset pagination: query.setFirstResult((page - 1) * size).setMaxResults(size) adds LIMIT/OFFSET (or FETCH FIRST). Always combine with a deterministic order by (including a unique tiebreaker such as the id) or pages overlap.
• Pagination with collection fetch joins is dangerous: Hibernate cannot limit in SQL and logs HHH000104: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory (loads everything!). Paginate the root ids first, then fetch children (see performance section) or use batch fetching.
• Keyset (seek) pagination (where (created_at, id) < (:lastCreated, :lastId) order by created_at desc, id desc limit 20) stays fast on deep pages; offset gets slower as the offset grows.

intermediate.content:
Aggregates, joins and subqueries

• Aggregate functions: count, sum, avg, min, max with group by and having. count(c) returns Long; sum/avg return Long/Double/BigDecimal depending on the type (watch for null when there are no rows).
• Joins: join (inner), left join, join fetch (also initialise the association), join on unrelated entities with on (Hibernate 5.1+/JPA 2.1). Alias everything; avoid cartesian products.
• Subqueries: where c.price > (select avg(c2.price) from Course c2), exists (...), in (...). Prefer exists over in for correlated checks.

expert.content:
Projections and DTO projections

• Loading full entities when you only need a few columns wastes memory and prevents the database from using covering indexes. A projection selects only some fields: scalar (select c.id, c.title → Object[]/Tuple), or a DTO projection.
• DTO projection in JPQL: select new com.app.CourseSummary(c.id, c.title, c.price) from Course c (or with Java records in Hibernate 6 you can omit new using Tuple/@Query result mapping). Spring Data interface projections (interface CourseView { Long getId(); String getTitle(); }) and class-based projections generate the SELECT list automatically. DTOs are read-only, not managed (no dirty checking, no lazy loading): perfect for list/search screens and APIs.

interviewQA: Why must pagination queries have an ORDER BY?
Without a deterministic order the database may return rows in any order, so pages can repeat or skip rows. Add a unique tiebreaker such as the id.
What is the problem with pagination and join fetch of a collection?

The SQL result has one row per child, so the database cannot apply LIMIT per parent; Hibernate warns HHH000104 and paginates in memory after loading everything. Paginate parent ids first, then fetch the children.
Why use DTO projections?
They select only the needed columns, avoid managed entities (memory, dirty checking, lazy loading) and decouple the API from the entity model, which is ideal for read-only list and search screens.

topics.name: First-Level Cache (Persistence Context)

beginner.content:
What the first-level cache is

• The first-level (L1) cache is the persistence context of a Session/EntityManager: always on, per session, not shared, cannot be disabled. It stores every managed entity by (entity type, id).
• Effects: repeated find(Course.class, 1L) in one transaction run one SELECT; the same Java instance is returned (identity guarantee); queries that return entities first check the cache by id for the returned rows (but a JPQL query itself always hits the database).
• Lifetime = the unit of work. In Spring it is the @Transactional method; each non-transactional repository call gets its own short-lived context.

intermediate.content:
Consequences and pitfalls

• Stale reads inside a long session: another transaction may change the row, but you keep reading the cached state; use refresh() or shorter transactions, or optimistic locking.
• Memory growth in batch jobs: every loaded entity stays in the context: flush() + clear() periodically, use StatelessSession, or stream with setReadOnly(true).
• Dirty-checking cost: at flush Hibernate compares every managed entity with its loaded snapshot; thousands of managed entities make commits slow. Use read-only transactions/queries (@Transactional(readOnly = true), QueryHints.HINT_READONLY) so Hibernate skips snapshots.
• Bulk JPQL/native updates bypass L1: managed entities become stale: clear() or refresh() afterwards (@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true) in Spring Data).

expert.content:
Inspecting and controlling L1

• em.contains(entity) (is it managed?), em.detach(entity) (evict one), em.clear() (evict all), em.flush(), em.refresh(); with Hibernate session.evict(entity) (= detach) and session.getStatistics().getEntityCount() (managed entity count).
• Rule of thumb: one request = one transaction = one persistence context; never keep a Session open across requests or in a singleton (a "global" EntityManager grows forever and is not thread-safe). The shared @PersistenceContext proxy is safe because it delegates to the current transaction's context.

interviewQA: What is the first-level cache?

The persistence context of a Session/EntityManager: a mandatory, per-session cache of managed entities keyed by type and id, giving identity guarantees and avoiding repeated SELECTs for the same entity within a unit of work.
Can you disable the first-level cache?
No, it is integral to the persistence context. You can limit it with clear()/detach(), StatelessSession (no persistence context) or read-only mode.
Why is memory a concern in batch processing with Hibernate?
Every entity loaded or persisted stays in the persistence context and is dirty-checked at flush. Flush and clear periodically (or use a StatelessSession) to keep memory and flush time constant.

topics.name: Second-Level Cache, Query Cache, Providers, Eviction and Configuration

beginner.content:
The second-level (L2) cache

• The second-level cache is optional and shared across sessions within a SessionFactory (an application instance). Hibernate stores entity state ("dehydrated" column values) by id; a find() miss in L1 checks L2 before the database. Reduces DB reads for read-mostly reference data (countries, categories, courses catalogue).
• Lookup order for find(id): L1 (session) → L2 (SessionFactory) → database.
• It must be enabled and each entity/collection opted in. Cached state is invalidated automatically when Hibernate changes the entity (but not by external SQL, bulk updates without notification, or other applications writing the table).

intermediate.content:
Concurrency strategies and cache providers

StrategyUse
READ_ONLYNever-changing data (lookup tables): fastest, no locking
NONSTRICT_READ_WRITERarely changing; small window of stale data accepted
READ_WRITEData that changes; soft locks keep reads consistent (default choice)
TRANSACTIONALFull transactional caches (JTA)
• Cache providers (Hibernate integrates through JCache/JSR-107): Ehcache 3 (most common), Caffeine (via JCache), Infinispan (clustered), Hazelcast (distributed), Redis via Redisson (distributed, good for multiple app instances). The built-in default is a no-op: you must add a provider.
• In a clustered/microservice deployment, a local L2 cache per instance can serve stale data after another instance writes: use a distributed provider, short TTLs, or cache only truly static data.
codeExamples:
<!-- ehcache.xml (JCache) -->
<config xmlns="http://www.ehcache.org/v3" xmlns:jsr107="http://www.ehcache.org/v3/jsr107">
  <service><jsr107:defaults enable-statistics="true"/></service>
  <cache alias="courses">
    <expiry><ttl unit="minutes">30</ttl></expiry>
    <resources><heap unit="entries">1000</heap></resources>
  </cache>
  <cache alias="default-query-results-region">
    <expiry><ttl unit="minutes">5</ttl></expiry>
    <resources><heap unit="entries">500</heap></resources>
  </cache>
</config>

// Redisson (distributed L2 cache for several service instances)
// hibernate.cache.region.factory_class=org.redisson.hibernate.RedissonRegionFactory
// hibernate.cache.redisson.config=redisson.yaml

expert.content:
Query cache, eviction, invalidation and monitoring

• Query cache: caches the result ids of a query (plus parameters) and relies on L2 for entity data. Enable with hibernate.cache.use_query_cache=true and opt in per query: .setHint("org.hibernate.cacheable", true) / Spring @QueryHints. It is invalidated whenever any table in the query is modified (timestamps), so it helps only for queries over rarely changing tables; for frequently written tables it adds overhead.
• Eviction: sessionFactory.getCache().evictEntityData(Course.class, id), evictAllRegions(), evictQueryRegions(), TTL/size in the provider. Invalidation: automatic on Hibernate-driven writes; for external changes or bulk JPQL updates evict manually or publish an event to evict (clustered setups).
• Monitor hit ratio with Statistics: getSecondLevelCacheHitCount()/MissCount()/PutCount(). A low hit ratio means the cache costs memory for no benefit: remove it. Measure before and after.
• Do not cache: frequently changing entities, large collections, sensitive data, anything with strict freshness needs (balances, inventory).

interviewQA: First-level vs second-level cache?

L1 is the session's persistence context: mandatory, per session, not shared. L2 is an optional cache shared by all sessions of a SessionFactory, configured per entity/collection with a provider; lookups go L1, then L2, then the database.
What does the query cache store and when does it help?

It stores the list of result ids for a query and its parameters (entity data comes from L2). It is invalidated when any table in the query is modified, so it helps only for queries over rarely changing tables.
What are the risks of a second-level cache in microservices?

Per-instance local caches can serve stale data after another instance writes, and external changes bypass invalidation. Use distributed providers, short TTLs, or cache only static data, and monitor the hit ratio.

topics.name: The N+1 Problem, Fetch Joins, Entity Graphs and Batch Fetching

beginner.content:
What is the N+1 query problem?

• You run 1 query to load N parents, then N more queries (one per parent) to load a lazy association while iterating: N+1 round trips. With 1000 courses it means 1001 queries instead of 1 or 2: the most common Hibernate performance bug.
• Causes: lazy collections/proxies accessed in a loop (or in toString/mapper/JSON serialisation), EAGER associations with JPQL (Hibernate loads the parent with your query, then each association with extra selects), Open Session In View hiding it until production.
• Detect: enable SQL logging and look for repeating statements; use Hibernate statistics or a datasource proxy (datasource-proxy, hypersistence-utils SQLStatementCountValidator) to assert query counts in tests.

intermediate.content:
Solutions: fetch joins and entity graphs

• join fetch loads the association in the same SQL join: select c from Course c join fetch c.category (to-one: safe) or left join fetch c.lessons (collection: duplicates parents, so use distinct; Hibernate 6 de-duplicates automatically).
• Rules: you can fetch join only one collection ("bag") safely per query: two List collections cause MultipleBagFetchException and a Cartesian product; use Sets carefully or split into several queries. Do not combine collection fetch joins with pagination.
• @EntityGraph (JPA 2.1) declares what to fetch per use case without changing JPQL; Spring Data: @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"category", "lessons"}) on repository methods.

expert.content:
Batch fetching and the two-query pattern

• Batch fetching (@BatchSize(size = 32) or global hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=32) turns N lazy loads into N/32 queries using where course_id in (?, ?, ...): a cheap, global, safe improvement that works with pagination. Subselect fetching (@Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT)) loads all collections of previously loaded parents in one query.
• Two-query pattern for paginated collections: query 1 paginates the parent ids/entities; query 2 loads children with where c.id in :ids (join fetch) and merges (or let batch fetching do it).
• For list screens prefer DTO projections (joined/aggregated in SQL) over loading graphs.

interviewQA: What is the N+1 query problem and how do you fix it?

One query loads N parents and then N extra queries load each lazy association. Fix with fetch joins, entity graphs, batch fetching (@BatchSize / default_batch_fetch_size), or DTO projections, and assert query counts in tests.
Why not fetch join several collections at once?
Fetching more than one List (bag) causes MultipleBagFetchException and a Cartesian product that multiplies rows. Fetch one collection per query or use batch fetching for the others.
join fetch vs EntityGraph?

Both fetch associations eagerly for a query. join fetch is written in the query itself; an EntityGraph is declared separately and applied to a query or repository method, letting you reuse the same query with different fetch plans.

topics.name: JDBC Batching, Connection Pooling and SQL Logging

beginner.content:
JDBC batching

• By default every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE is a separate round trip. JDBC batching groups statements into batches: hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50. It works for writes only and requires: a generator that does not force immediate execution (SEQUENCE, not IDENTITY), hibernate.order_inserts=true and hibernate.order_updates=true (so same-table statements are adjacent), hibernate.jdbc.batch_versioned_data=true.
• Driver flags: MySQL rewriteBatchedStatements=true; PostgreSQL reWriteBatchedInserts=true.
• Process large imports in chunks with flush() + clear() every batch size; consider JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate or StatelessSession for millions of rows.

intermediate.content:
Connection pooling (HikariCP)

• Opening a database connection is expensive, so apps use a connection pool; Spring Boot's default is HikariCP. Hibernate borrows a connection when a transaction/query starts and returns it at the end: a long transaction = a connection held for its whole duration.
• Sizing: smaller is better. Starting point: connections ≈ (core_count × 2) + effective_spindle_count for the database across all app instances (often 10-20 per instance). Many instances × big pools can overwhelm the DB (max_connections). Symptoms of exhaustion: threads waiting for HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available.
• Tune maximum-pool-size, minimum-idle, connection-timeout (fail fast), max-lifetime (below the DB/ firewall timeout), leak-detection-threshold (find unclosed/long-held connections). Avoid Open Session In View (it holds the connection during view rendering) and remote calls inside transactions.
codeExamples:
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=15
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=5000          # fail fast instead of piling up requests
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1700000             # slightly below the database/proxy idle limit
spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=20000   # log a stack trace for connections held > 20 s
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

# Metrics: hikaricp_connections_active / _pending / _timeout_total (Micrometer) -> alert on pending > 0
// BAD: remote call holds a DB connection
@Transactional
public void checkout(Order o) { repo.save(o); paymentClient.charge(o); }     // slow HTTP call while the connection is checked out
// BETTER: do the remote call outside, or use the outbox pattern

expert.content:
SQL logging and statistics

• Never trust, always check the SQL. Development: logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG prints statements; logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE shows bind values; hibernate.format_sql=true pretty-prints. Avoid spring.jpa.show-sql=true in production (stdout, no bind values) and avoid logging all SQL in production (cost).
• Statistics: hibernate.generate_statistics=true exposes counts (queries, entity loads, cache hits, slow queries via hibernate.session.events.log.LOG_QUERIES_SLOWER_THAN_MS) and integrates with Micrometer/Actuator.
• Slow query log at database level (MySQL slow_query_log, PostgreSQL log_min_duration_statement) + EXPLAIN ANALYZE for the real plan. APM tools (Datadog, New Relic, Glowroot) show per-endpoint query counts.

interviewQA: Why does IDENTITY prevent JDBC insert batching?

The identifier is created by the database at insert time, so Hibernate must execute each INSERT immediately to read the key and cannot queue them in a batch. SEQUENCE ids are fetched in advance, allowing batching.
How big should a HikariCP pool be?

Small: roughly a couple of times the database server's core count in total across all instances (commonly 10-20 per instance). Larger pools do not add throughput and can overload the database; keep transactions short so connections return quickly.
How do you see what SQL Hibernate generates?
Enable the org.hibernate.SQL logger (and the bind logger for parameters), format_sql, Hibernate statistics, or a datasource proxy; assert query counts in tests and use EXPLAIN on slow statements.

topics.name: Query Optimization, Indexing, Read-Only Queries and Avoiding Eager Loading

beginner.content:
Query optimisation checklist

• Select only what you need: DTO/interface projections for lists; avoid loading entities for read-only screens. Fetch what you need in one go: fetch joins/entity graphs/batch size. Paginate everything user-facing; never return unbounded lists.
• Avoid findAll() on big tables, count() on huge tables per request (cache or approximate), functions on indexed columns in where (lower(email) defeats an index unless a functional index exists), like '%text' (leading wildcard), or chains, select distinct on big graphs, and in with thousands of values (chunk it).
• Prefer set-based bulk operations over loading entities one by one; use exists for presence checks (existsById, existsByEmail) instead of count or loading.

intermediate.content:
Indexing

• Indexes make lookups fast but slow writes and use space: index the columns you filter, join and sort on. Foreign key columns used in joins (enrollment.course_id) need an index (PostgreSQL does not create one automatically; MySQL InnoDB does for FKs). Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: (student_id, course_id) serves queries on student_id and on both, not on course_id alone.
• Declare them in migrations (Flyway); @Table(indexes = ...) documents them and is used for schema generation in tests. Check usage with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE); drop unused indexes. Covering indexes (include selected columns) enable index-only scans for projections.
• Unique constraints (@UniqueConstraint) both enforce rules and create indexes.

expert.content:
Read-only queries, pagination optimisation and avoiding unnecessary eager loading

• Read-only transactions/queries skip the dirty-checking snapshot and flush: @Transactional(readOnly = true) for all query-only service methods (also hints the driver/DB: routing to a replica, MySQL read-only transaction). Use setReadOnly(true)/HINT_READ_ONLY on queries; DTO projections are inherently read-only.
• Pagination optimisation: use keyset pagination for deep pages; use Slice (no count query) when you only need "next page?"; cache or estimate totals; avoid count(*) with big joins (use a simplified count query); fetch ids first then entities for collection fetches.
• Avoid unnecessary eager loading: audit mappings with grep -R "FetchType.EAGER|@ManyToOne$|@OneToOne$" (remember the defaults!); all to-one associations explicit LAZY; large LOB fields lazy or in a separate table; never EAGER on collections; use projections for UI lists. Re-check after adding associations: a new EAGER mapping changes every query of that entity.

interviewQA: How do you optimise a slow Hibernate query?

Look at the generated SQL and the database execution plan; select only needed columns (projections), fix N+1 with fetch joins/batch fetching, add the right indexes, paginate, avoid functions/leading wildcards on indexed columns, use read-only transactions and cache stable data.
Why use readOnly = true on query methods?
Hibernate skips dirty checking and snapshots (less memory and CPU) and avoids unnecessary flushes; it also signals intent to the database/driver and routing layers.
Page vs Slice?
Page runs an extra count query to know the total pages and elements; Slice only knows whether a next page exists, avoiding the count and making it cheaper for infinite scroll.

topics.name: ACID, Hibernate Transactions, Spring @Transactional, Propagation and Isolation

beginner.content:
ACID properties

PropertyMeaningProvided by
AtomicityAll operations succeed or none doTransaction commit/rollback, undo log
ConsistencyConstraints hold before and after (valid state to valid state)DB constraints + application rules
IsolationConcurrent transactions do not see each other's partial workLocking / MVCC, isolation level
DurabilityCommitted data survives crashesWrite-ahead log, fsync
• Hibernate does not implement ACID itself: it uses the database transaction (via JDBC) and adds a unit-of-work/flush mechanism on top.

intermediate.content:
Spring @Transactional

• @Transactional on a public method of a Spring bean creates a proxy that begins a transaction (obtains a connection, creates the persistence context), runs the method and commits, or rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException/Error); checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor.
• Put it on the service layer (one business operation = one transaction), not on controllers or repositories. Attributes: readOnly, propagation, isolation, timeout, rollbackFor/noRollbackFor. Class-level + method override is common.
• Self-invocation and private/final methods bypass the proxy; @Transactional on interfaces vs classes: annotate classes. Use TransactionTemplate for programmatic control; @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) to react after commit.

expert.content:
Propagation and isolation levels

REQUIRES_NEWAlways start a new, independent transaction; suspend the current one (audit logs, outbox that must commit even if the caller rolls back)
SUPPORTSJoin if one exists, else run non-transactionally
MANDATORYMust run inside a transaction, else exception
NOT_SUPPORTEDRun without a transaction (suspend the current)
NEVERFail if a transaction exists
NESTEDSavepoint inside the current transaction (JDBC savepoints)
IsolationPreventsAllows
READ_UNCOMMITTEDnothingdirty, non-repeatable, phantom reads
READ_COMMITTED (PostgreSQL/Oracle default)dirty readsnon-repeatable and phantom reads
REPEATABLE_READ (MySQL InnoDB default)dirty and non-repeatable readsphantoms (InnoDB largely prevents via gap locks)
