interviewQA: What are the ACID properties?
Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives failures).
REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW?

REQUIRED joins the caller's transaction (one commit/rollback for all); REQUIRES_NEW suspends it and runs an independent transaction that commits or rolls back on its own, useful for audit/outbox records.
What does the isolation level control?

How much concurrent transactions can see of each other: dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads. Higher levels (REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE) give stronger guarantees with less concurrency and possible retries.

topics.name: Optimistic and Pessimistic Locking, @Version and Deadlock Handling

beginner.content:
Lost updates and optimistic locking

• Lost update: two users load the same row, both change it, the second commit overwrites the first without noticing. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: add a @Version field (int/long/Instant); Hibernate adds where id=? and version=? to every UPDATE/DELETE and increments the version. If 0 rows are updated, someone else changed it: OptimisticLockException (Spring: ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException).
• No database locks are held: great scalability, ideal for web apps with user think time. Handle the exception: retry (for system operations) or tell the user to reload (HTTP 409 Conflict). Send the version to the client (ETag/field) so conflicts across requests are detected.

intermediate.content:
Pessimistic locking

• Pessimistic locking locks the rows in the database (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so others wait. Use when conflicts are frequent or the cost of failure is high (inventory decrement, seat booking, balance transfer) and transactions are short.
• JPA: em.find(Course.class, id, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) (FOR UPDATE), PESSIMISTIC_READ (FOR SHARE), PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT; Spring Data: @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) on a query. Set a lock timeout (jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout hint) and use SKIP LOCKED (hibernate.jdbc.., Hibernate hint jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout = -2) for work queues.
• Also available: OPTIMISTIC / OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT lock modes to verify/bump a version of entities you only read.

expert.content:
Choosing a strategy and handling deadlocks

Optimistic (@Version)Pessimistic (FOR UPDATE)
Conflict handlingDetected at commit; exceptionPrevented; others wait
ThroughputHigh (no locks)Lower (blocking)
Best whenConflicts are rare, long user think timeConflicts frequent, short critical section
RisksRetries / user conflictsDeadlocks, lock waits, held connections
• Deadlock: transaction A holds row 1 and waits for row 2; B holds row 2 and waits for row 1. The database detects it and aborts one (40001/40P01, Spring DeadlockLoserDataAccessException/CannotAcquireLockException). Prevent by locking rows in a consistent order (sort ids), keeping transactions short, using the lowest necessary isolation, and avoiding user interaction inside transactions. Handle with retry and backoff of the whole transaction.
• Atomic updates often avoid locking altogether: update course set seats = seats - 1 where id = ? and seats > 0 (check rows affected).

interviewQA: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?

Optimistic locking uses a @Version column and detects conflicting updates at commit (exception), holding no locks; pessimistic locking locks rows in the database (SELECT FOR UPDATE) so concurrent transactions wait. Use optimistic by default and pessimistic for hot, short critical sections.
What does @Version do?

Hibernate adds the version to the WHERE clause of UPDATE/DELETE and increments it; if no row matches, another transaction changed the entity and an optimistic lock exception is thrown, preventing lost updates.
How do you prevent and handle deadlocks?

Lock rows in a consistent order, keep transactions short, avoid unnecessary locks (use atomic updates), and retry the whole transaction with backoff when the database aborts one as the deadlock victim.

topics.name: Dirty Checking, Write-Behind and Flush Modes

beginner.content:
Dirty checking

• When an entity is loaded, Hibernate keeps a snapshot of its state ("loaded state"). At flush time it compares every managed entity's current state with its snapshot; each difference becomes an UPDATE automatically: no save() call is needed.
• Cost: proportional to the number of managed entities × properties. Reduce with read-only entities/queries, DTO projections, clear() in batches and bytecode enhancement (dirty tracking by instrumentation: hibernate.enhancer.enableDirtyTracking).
• By default UPDATE statements include all columns (statement reuse); @DynamicUpdate includes only changed columns (useful for wide tables or concurrent updates of different columns).

intermediate.content:
Write-behind (transactional write-behind)

• Hibernate does not execute SQL when you call persist/remove or set a field: it queues the changes in the action queue and sends them at flush time (usually at commit), in a safe order: inserts, updates, collection removals/updates/inserts, deletes. Benefits: fewer round trips, JDBC batching, no work for changes that cancel out (persist then remove).
• Consequences: SQL errors (constraint violations) appear at flush/commit, not at the line that caused them: call flush() inside a try/catch when you need the error handled locally; execution order differs from your code order (hibernate.order_inserts); exceptions can surface far from the cause.
• IDENTITY inserts are the exception (executed immediately).

expert.content:
Flush modes

• FlushModeType.AUTO (default): Hibernate flushes before a query whose results could be affected by pending changes (it checks the query's tables), and at commit: queries see your uncommitted changes. COMMIT: flush only at commit (faster, but queries may miss pending changes). Hibernate-native: MANUAL (only when you call flush(): ideal for read-only sessions) and ALWAYS (before every query).
• Native SQL queries: Hibernate cannot know the affected tables, so it flushes everything before them unless you declare query spaces; with COMMIT mode flush manually first.
• A flush at an unexpected time can also run unintended updates (an entity modified earlier and forgotten): keep transactions focused and entities clean.

interviewQA: What is dirty checking?

Hibernate compares each managed entity with a snapshot taken when it was loaded and automatically issues UPDATE statements for changed entities at flush, so you do not call save() for managed entities.
What is the write-behind mechanism?

Hibernate queues entity changes in an action queue and executes the SQL at flush time (usually commit) in a defined order, reducing round trips and enabling batching; errors therefore surface at flush/commit.
AUTO vs COMMIT flush mode?
AUTO flushes pending changes before queries that might be affected, so queries see them; COMMIT flushes only at commit, which is faster but queries can miss uncommitted changes.

topics.name: Inheritance Mapping: Single Table, Joined, Table Per Class and MappedSuperclass

beginner.content:
Strategies at a glance

StrategyTablesPolymorphic queryProsCons
SINGLE_TABLE (default)One table for the whole hierarchy + discriminator column1 SELECT, no joinFastest, simpleSubclass columns must be nullable; wide, sparse table; no NOT NULL for subclass fields
JOINEDTable per class, joined by PK/FKJoins (or union) over the tablesNormalised, NOT NULL constraints, no sparse columnsJoins for every load; slower inserts (2+ statements)
TABLE_PER_CLASSA full table per concrete classUNION of all tablesNo joins for single-class queriesSlow polymorphic queries; no polymorphic FKs; ids must be unique across tables (no IDENTITY): avoid
@MappedSuperclassNot an entity: shares fields onlyNo polymorphic queries on the parentReuse common columns (id, audit)Cannot be queried or targeted by associations
• Default recommendation: SINGLE_TABLE for small hierarchies where performance matters, JOINED when you need strict constraints. Prefer composition over deep inheritance.

intermediate.content:
Single table and joined

• SINGLE_TABLE: all columns live in one table; @DiscriminatorColumn (DTYPE) + @DiscriminatorValue identify the subclass. JOINED: the child table's PK is also an FK to the parent (@PrimaryKeyJoinColumn); loading a subclass joins parent and child; a polymorphic query to the parent left-joins all subclasses.

expert.content:
@MappedSuperclass and practical advice

• @MappedSuperclass is the cleanest way to share common fields (id, version, audit timestamps) among unrelated entities without a polymorphic hierarchy; the parent is not an entity.
• Use @DiscriminatorFormula or @Any for special cases; mix inheritance with embeddables for value types. Polymorphic associations (@ManyToOne Content content) work with SINGLE_TABLE/JOINED; with TABLE_PER_CLASS they need unions.
• Pitfalls: lazy proxies of an abstract parent are of the parent's proxy class, so instanceof VideoLesson fails on a proxy: use Hibernate.unproxy(x) or the visitor pattern; deep hierarchies hurt queries and schema; enum type fields (type + nullable columns) can be simpler than inheritance.

interviewQA: Which inheritance strategy should you choose?

SINGLE_TABLE for speed and simplicity (accepting nullable subclass columns), JOINED for a normalised schema with NOT NULL constraints (accepting joins), and avoid TABLE_PER_CLASS. Use @MappedSuperclass to share common fields.
What is @MappedSuperclass?
A non-entity superclass whose mapped fields are inherited by entity subclasses (for example id, version and audit columns); it has no table of its own and cannot be queried or referenced.
Why does instanceof fail on a lazy proxy?
The proxy is a generated subclass of the declared type (the parent), not of the real subclass; unproxy it with Hibernate.unproxy or avoid type checks in favour of polymorphic methods.

topics.name: Composite Primary Keys, Custom Types and Attribute Converters

beginner.content:
Composite primary keys: @EmbeddedId vs @IdClass

• A composite key has several columns (a link table with (student_id, course_id)). The key class must be Serializable with equals() and hashCode() and a no-arg constructor.
• @EmbeddedId: the key is an @Embeddable object held as a single field (enrollment.getId().getStudentId()): cleaner, reusable in queries (e.id.studentId). @IdClass: the entity declares the key fields itself and points to a plain key class: queries use e.studentId; handy with legacy schemas and for @Id @ManyToOne derived keys. Use @MapsId to derive key parts from relationships.
• Prefer a surrogate key (@GeneratedValue) plus a unique constraint for new schemas: simpler repositories, easier foreign keys.

intermediate.content:
Attribute converters

• AttributeConverter<X, Y> converts a Java attribute type X to a database column type Y and back: encrypted strings, comma-separated lists, value objects (Email, Money), booleans stored as 'Y'/'N', JSON in a text column, custom enums with codes. Apply per attribute (@Convert(converter = ...)) or globally with @Converter(autoApply = true).
• Converters cannot be used on @Id, @Version, relationships or @Enumerated/@Temporal attributes. They run on every read/write: keep them fast, null-safe and deterministic; JPQL comparisons use the converted value.

expert.content:
Custom types and modern alternatives

• Hibernate 6 provides @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) to map a Java object/Map to a JSON/JSONB column (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle), @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.ARRAY) for arrays, @JavaType/@JdbcType for custom combinations, UserType for fully custom persistence (legacy @Type), plus native enum and java.time support.
• Use JSON columns for flexible, rarely queried attributes (settings, metadata); keep relational columns for what you filter and join on. Index JSON paths where needed (PostgreSQL GIN).
• @Formula("(select count(*) from enrollment e where e.course_id = id)") maps a read-only computed value (use sparingly).

interviewQA: @EmbeddedId vs @IdClass?

Both model composite keys. @EmbeddedId holds the key as one embeddable object field (queries use e.id.part); @IdClass leaves key fields directly on the entity and references a separate key class (queries use e.part). Key classes need equals, hashCode and Serializable.
What is an AttributeConverter?
A JPA component that converts an entity attribute type to a database column type and back (encryption, lists, value objects, Y/N booleans); applied per attribute or automatically with autoApply.
How can you store JSON in a column with Hibernate 6?
Use @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) on a Map or POJO attribute, mapped to jsonb/json columns, and index paths in the database if you query them.

topics.name: Auditing, Soft Deletes, Hibernate Filters and Entity Listeners

beginner.content:
Entity listeners and lifecycle callbacks

• JPA callbacks: @PrePersist, @PostPersist, @PreUpdate, @PostUpdate, @PreRemove, @PostRemove, @PostLoad, on the entity or in a separate listener class (@EntityListeners). Use for timestamps, default values, validation and simple events.
• Rules: callbacks run inside the persistence context: do not call EntityManager operations or touch other entities in them; they are not triggered by bulk JPQL/native updates. Hibernate adds @CreationTimestamp/@UpdateTimestamp and @CurrentTimestamp.

intermediate.content:
Auditing: history of changes (Envers) and soft deletes

• Hibernate Envers (hibernate-envers, @Audited) records every change in *_aud tables with a revision number, so you can query history (AuditReaderFactory.get(em).find(Course.class, id, revision)) and who/when with a custom revision entity. Great for compliance; costs extra writes and storage.
• Soft delete: instead of DELETE, mark the row deleted and hide it from queries. Hibernate 6.4+ provides @SoftDelete; older: @SQLDelete(sql = "update course set deleted = true where id = ? and version = ?") + @SQLRestriction("deleted = false") (@Where in older versions). Benefits: recovery, audit trail, referential integrity. Costs: every query must exclude deleted rows, unique constraints need to include the flag (or partial unique index), data grows (archive job).

expert.content:
Hibernate filters

• A filter adds a runtime-enabled WHERE condition to entity loads and queries: @FilterDef(name, parameters) + @Filter(name, condition) on the entity, enabled per session with session.enableFilter("name").setParameter(...). Use for multi-tenant row filtering (tenant_id = :tenantId), "active only", date visibility, and per-user data scopes.
• Limits: filters apply to queries and entity loads but not to find() by id (older versions) and not to native SQL; enable them in a Spring AOP aspect or request filter inside the transaction (the session must be the same one used by the repositories).

interviewQA: What is the difference between entity listeners and Envers?
Listeners/callbacks run custom code at lifecycle events (timestamps, validation); Envers automatically stores a full history of every audited entity change in audit tables with revisions.
How do you implement soft deletes?

Mark rows as deleted instead of deleting them and exclude them from queries: Hibernate 6.4+ @SoftDelete, or @SQLDelete (rewrites DELETE to UPDATE) with @SQLRestriction("deleted = false"); handle unique constraints with partial indexes.
What are Hibernate filters used for?
To apply a parameterised WHERE condition to queries dynamically per session, for example tenant isolation, "active only" or visibility rules, enabled with session.enableFilter().

topics.name: Multi-Tenancy, Schema Generation and Stored Procedures

beginner.content:
Multi-tenancy

• Multi-tenancy serves many customers (tenants) from one application. Isolation models: database per tenant (strongest isolation, costly), schema per tenant (good balance), shared schema with a discriminator column (tenant_id; cheapest, needs strict filtering; PostgreSQL Row Level Security adds protection).
• Hibernate supports DATABASE/SCHEMA strategies with CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver (which tenant is this request?) and MultiTenantConnectionProvider (which connection/schema), and discriminator-based via @TenantId (Hibernate 6) or filters.
• Keep the tenant in a request-scoped context (from the JWT/subdomain), propagate it to async tasks and run migrations per tenant.

intermediate.content:
Database schema generation

• spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto / hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto: none, validate (check entities vs schema: use in production), update (alters the schema: unsafe, cannot drop/rename, never in production), create, create-drop (tests with H2/Testcontainers). The JPA standard properties jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.* can export scripts (create / drop files) to bootstrap migrations.
• Production practice: schema is owned by Flyway/Liquibase migrations (versioned, reviewed, repeatable); Hibernate only validates. Generate a first draft DDL from entities, then edit it by hand.
codeExamples:
# development (throw-away database)
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create-drop
# tests with Testcontainers
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create
# production
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

# generate DDL scripts from entities (then move into Flyway)
spring.jpa.properties.jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.scripts.action=create
spring.jpa.properties.jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.scripts.create-target=build/schema.sql

// programmatic export
new SchemaExport().setFormat(true).setOutputFile("schema.sql").createOnly(EnumSet.of(TargetType.SCRIPT), metadata);

expert.content:
Stored procedures and functions

• Call database logic from JPA with @NamedStoredProcedureQuery or programmatically: em.createStoredProcedureQuery("apply_discount"), registerStoredProcedureParameter(...) (IN/OUT/INOUT/REF_CURSOR), execute(), getOutputParameterValue(...). Spring Data: @Procedure(procedureName = "apply_discount").
• Alternatives for scalar functions: native query select my_function(:x); Hibernate 6 can register custom functions (FunctionContributor) to use them in HQL.
• Trade-offs: logic in the database is fast for set-based work and legacy systems, but hard to version/test/port; keep business rules in the application where possible; procedures run in the same transaction and connection as the persistence context (flush first).

interviewQA: Which multi-tenancy models exist?

Database per tenant (strong isolation), schema per tenant (good balance) and shared schema with a tenant discriminator column (cheapest, needs strict filtering such as @TenantId, filters or row-level security).
Why shouldn't ddl-auto=update be used in production?
It cannot handle renames, drops or data migrations reliably and can change the schema unexpectedly. Use versioned Flyway/Liquibase migrations and set ddl-auto to validate.
How do you call a stored procedure from Hibernate/JPA?
With @NamedStoredProcedureQuery or em.createStoredProcedureQuery, registering IN/OUT parameters and calling execute(); in Spring Data JPA use @Procedure on a repository method.

topics.name: Spring Data JPA: Repository Interfaces, JpaRepository, Derived Queries, @Query and Native Queries

beginner.content:
Repository interfaces

• Spring Data JPA removes DAO boilerplate: declare an interface and Spring generates the implementation (a proxy backed by SimpleJpaRepository) using Hibernate/JPA.
• Hierarchy: Repository (marker) → CrudRepository (save, findById, findAll, deleteById, existsById, count) → ListCrudRepository/PagingAndSortingRepository → JpaRepository (adds flush, saveAndFlush, saveAll, deleteAllInBatch, getReferenceById, findAll(Sort), findAll(Pageable)) and JpaSpecificationExecutor for Specifications.
• Enable with Spring Boot (auto-configured) or @EnableJpaRepositories; repositories are transactional by default (readOnly for reads, read-write for writes).

intermediate.content:
Derived query keywords

• Long method names become unreadable: switch to @Query beyond 2-3 conditions. Startup validates derived names against properties (typos fail fast).

expert.content:
@Query, native queries and modifying queries

• @Query("select c from Course c where ...") with named parameters (@Param) or positional; SpEL: #{#entityName}; nativeQuery = true for SQL (add countQuery for pagination; interface projections for results).
• Modifying queries (update/delete) need @Modifying (and run in a transaction: @Transactional); consider clearAutomatically = true because bulk statements bypass the persistence context.
• Query hints (@QueryHints), locking (@Lock), fetching (@EntityGraph), projections (interface/record DTO), and query by example (QueryByExampleExecutor) for simple dynamic filters.

interviewQA: What does JpaRepository give you?

CRUD, paging and sorting methods plus JPA-specific operations (flush, saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch, getReferenceById) implemented automatically by Spring Data on top of Hibernate; you add query methods by naming convention or @Query.
Derived query methods vs @Query?
Derived methods generate JPQL from the method name (good for 1-3 simple conditions); @Query gives explicit control for joins, projections, aggregates, native SQL and readability when names get long.
Why does a @Modifying query need clearAutomatically?
Bulk update/delete statements bypass the persistence context, leaving managed entities stale; clearing (or refreshing) afterwards prevents reading outdated state.

topics.name: Specifications, Pageable, Page vs Slice, DTO Mapping and Entity-to-DTO Conversion

beginner.content:
Specifications for dynamic queries

• A Specification<T> wraps a Criteria Predicate; extend the repository with JpaSpecificationExecutor<T> and combine specs with and(), or(), not(). Ideal for search/filter screens where any combination of filters may be supplied. Use the metamodel (Course_.title) for type safety. For very complex cases consider Querydsl or jOOQ.

intermediate.content:
Pageable, Page vs Slice, Sort

• Pageable (PageRequest.of(page, size, Sort), zero-based) lets any repository method paginate and sort; in controllers it is bound from ?page=0&size=20&sort=title,asc (set a maximum page size: spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size=100).
Page<T>Slice<T>List<T> with Pageable
Count queryYes (extra select count)No (fetches size+1 to know if there is a next)No
Knows total elements/pagesYesNo (hasNext() only)No
UseNumbered pagination UIsInfinite scroll, "load more"When you do not need metadata
• Return a stable DTO page (PagedResponse) rather than the Spring Page JSON (its shape changes between versions; Spring Data 3.3 warns about serialising PageImpl directly: use PagedModel/@EnableSpringDataWebSupport(pageSerializationMode = VIA_DTO)).

expert.content:
DTO mapping and entity-to-DTO conversion

• Never expose entities from controllers: it leaks the schema, triggers lazy loading during JSON serialisation (LazyInitializationException/N+1), causes infinite recursion in bidirectional relations, couples API to persistence and allows mass assignment (clients setting fields like role). Use DTOs (Java records) for requests and responses.
• Conversion options: manual mapper methods (clear, fast, recommended for small apps), MapStruct (compile-time generated mappers: fast, type-safe; excellent default), ModelMapper (reflection: slower, runtime errors). Prefer projections for read models: select straight into DTOs and skip entities entirely.
• Map inside the transaction (lazy associations available) or fetch what the DTO needs up front; map incoming DTOs to entities in the service, validating (@Valid) and never trusting ids or roles from the client.

interviewQA: Page vs Slice?
Page executes an additional count query and exposes total elements and pages; Slice only fetches one extra row to know whether a next page exists, which is cheaper for infinite scroll.
Why should entities not be returned directly from REST controllers?

It exposes the internal schema, can trigger lazy loading or N+1 during serialisation, causes recursion in bidirectional associations, couples the API to persistence and enables mass assignment. Return DTOs.
What are Specifications for?
Composable, reusable Criteria predicates for dynamic filtering: you combine optional filters with and/or and pass the result to repository.findAll(spec, pageable).

topics.name: Transactions, Database Configuration, Dialects, Flyway/Liquibase Migrations and Exception Handling

beginner.content:
Database configuration and dialects

• Spring Boot configures a DataSource (HikariCP), an EntityManagerFactory (Hibernate), a JpaTransactionManager and repositories from properties. Use profiles (application-dev.yml, application-prod.yml) and environment variables / secrets for credentials, never commit passwords.
• Dialect: the class that generates database-specific SQL (pagination syntax, types, functions, identity/sequence support). Hibernate 6 auto-detects it from the JDBC metadata, so do not set hibernate.dialect unless you must (custom dialect or version pinning). Known ones: MySQLDialect, PostgreSQLDialect, OracleDialect, SQLServerDialect, H2Dialect (Hibernate 6 removed version-specific subclasses such as MySQL8Dialect).
codeExamples:
# application-prod.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://${DB_HOST:localhost}:5432/javaschoollab
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    hikari: { maximum-pool-size: 15, connection-timeout: 5000 }
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc.time_zone: UTC                       # store and read timestamps in UTC
        default_batch_fetch_size: 32
        jdbc.batch_size: 50
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    locations: classpath:db/migration
# no hibernate.dialect: it is detected from the database metadata

intermediate.content:
Database migrations with Flyway or Liquibase

• Migrations version the schema as code: reviewed in pull requests, applied automatically on startup, identical in every environment. Flyway: SQL files named V1__init.sql, V2__add_slug.sql in db/migration, a flyway_schema_history table with checksums; repeatable R__views.sql. Liquibase: XML/YAML/JSON/SQL changelogs with changesets, rollbacks and contexts.
• Rules: never edit an applied migration (checksum failure): add a new one; keep migrations backward compatible for rolling deployments (expand → migrate → contract: add a nullable column first, backfill, then enforce); test migrations on a copy of production; run with ddl-auto=validate; baseline existing databases (baselineOnMigrate).

expert.content:
Exception handling

• Spring translates persistence exceptions into its DataAccessException hierarchy (via @Repository proxies): DataIntegrityViolationException (unique/foreign key/not null), EmptyResultDataAccessException, IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException, ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException, CannotAcquireLockException, QueryTimeoutException, JpaSystemException; Hibernate-specific: LazyInitializationException, NonUniqueResultException, TransientObjectException, StaleObjectStateException.
• Handle them centrally with a @RestControllerAdvice mapping to HTTP statuses and clean messages (409 for conflicts/duplicates, 404, 422, 503 for pool exhaustion), log the cause and never leak SQL/constraint names to clients. Remember a transaction marked rollback-only: do not swallow exceptions inside @Transactional methods.

interviewQA: Why not set hibernate.dialect in Hibernate 6?
Hibernate 6 detects the dialect automatically from the JDBC connection metadata, including the database version; setting it manually is only needed for custom dialects or to pin behaviour.
Why use Flyway or Liquibase instead of ddl-auto=update?
Migrations give versioned, reviewed, repeatable schema changes with history and checksums; update cannot handle renames, drops or data migrations safely and behaves differently across environments.
How should persistence exceptions be handled in a REST API?

Translate them centrally with @RestControllerAdvice: unique/FK violations and optimistic lock failures to 409, missing rows to 404, database unavailability to 503, logging the cause but not leaking SQL details to clients.

topics.name: Interview Q&A: Fundamentals and Core APIs (131-138)

beginner.content:
How to answer well

• Interviewers test understanding, not memorisation: give the definition, the why, a tiny example and a pitfall you have seen. For each answer below, practise explaining what SQL Hibernate generates and when it executes.
• Questions covered here: What is Hibernate? What is ORM? Hibernate vs JPA, get() vs load() and modern alternatives, persist() vs merge(), save() vs saveOrUpdate(), first vs second-level cache, lazy vs eager loading.

intermediate.content:
Model answers

QuestionAnswer
What is Hibernate?An ORM framework and JPA implementation that maps Java objects to tables, generates SQL, manages the persistence context, caching, lazy loading, dirty checking and transactions on top of JDBC.
What is ORM?Object-Relational Mapping: automatic translation between an object model and a relational schema, solving the impedance mismatch (identity, inheritance, associations, types) so code works with objects instead of SQL and ResultSets.
Hibernate vs JPA?JPA is the specification (API and annotations); Hibernate is an implementation with extra features. Code against JPA (EntityManager) to stay provider-independent and use Hibernate-specific APIs deliberately.
get() vs load() (modern: find() vs getReference())get/find returns the entity or null, hitting the database immediately if not cached. load/getReference returns a lazy proxy without a query and throws EntityNotFoundException on first access if absent; use it to set foreign keys cheaply.
persist() vs merge()persist makes a transient instance managed (same object, INSERT); merge copies a detached/transient state onto a managed copy and returns it (SELECT then INSERT/UPDATE); the argument stays unmanaged.
save() vs saveOrUpdate()Legacy Hibernate: save always INSERTs and returns the id; saveOrUpdate decides insert/update from the id/version. Both are removed in Hibernate 6: use persist()/merge(); Spring Data's save() chooses based on isNew().
First-level vs second-level cacheL1: per session/persistence context, mandatory, identity guarantee. L2: optional, shared across sessions of a SessionFactory, per entity, needs a provider; lookup L1 → L2 → DB.
Lazy vs eager loadingLazy loads on first access (proxy/collection, needs open session); eager loads with the owner. Default: to-one eager, collections lazy; best practice: everything lazy and fetch explicitly per use case.

expert.content:
Follow-up questions to expect

• "Show me the SQL for find() followed by setPrice()": one SELECT and, at commit, one UPDATE (dirty checking).
• "What happens if you call persist() on a detached entity?" → PersistenceException: detached entity passed to persist.
• "When would getReference() save you a query?" → when only the id is needed to set a foreign key (enrollment.setCourse(em.getReference(...))).
• "Why is EAGER a problem?" → it cannot be turned off per query, causes N+1 and loads unneeded data.

interviewQA: What is Hibernate?

An open-source ORM framework and JPA implementation that maps entities to tables and automates SQL generation, caching, lazy loading, dirty checking and transaction-bound persistence contexts on top of JDBC.
get() vs load()?
get (find) returns the entity or null with an immediate query; load (getReference) returns a lazy proxy without a query and fails with an exception on first access if the row is missing.
persist() vs merge()?
persist attaches a new entity (same instance, INSERT); merge copies detached or new state onto a managed instance and returns that copy, issuing a SELECT and an INSERT or UPDATE.

topics.name: Interview Q&A: Performance, Concurrency and Troubleshooting (139-150)

beginner.content:
Questions 139-150

• What is the N+1 problem? What is dirty checking? What is the persistence context? What is cascading? What is orphan removal? What is optimistic locking? flush() vs commit()? EntityManager vs Session? How do you optimise slow queries? How do you handle bidirectional relationships? How does Hibernate generate SQL? How do you troubleshoot lazy initialization errors?
• These are the senior-level questions: tie every answer to a real incident (a slow endpoint caused by N+1, a lost update fixed with @Version).

intermediate.content:
Model answers

QuestionAnswer
N+1 problem1 query for N parents plus N queries for a lazy association. Fix: fetch join, entity graph, batch fetching, DTO projection; detect with SQL logs/statistics and query-count assertions in tests.
Dirty checkingAt flush Hibernate compares managed entities to their load-time snapshot and issues UPDATEs for changes, so no explicit save is needed; cost grows with managed entities (use read-only/projections/clear).
Persistence contextThe set of managed entities of an EntityManager/Session: first-level cache, identity map, change tracker and write-behind action queue; transaction-scoped in Spring.
CascadingPropagating persist/merge/remove/refresh/detach from parent to associated entities; use for composition only, never for shared aggregates or many-to-many removal.
Orphan removalDeletes a child when it is removed from the parent's collection; stronger than cascade REMOVE; mutate the collection, do not replace it.
Optimistic locking@Version column added to UPDATE/DELETE predicates; a conflict gives OptimisticLockException (retry or HTTP 409); no database locks held.
flush() vs commit()flush sends pending SQL inside the transaction (still rollback-able); commit flushes then makes the transaction durable and visible.
EntityManager vs SessionEntityManager is the JPA standard; Session extends it with Hibernate-only features (filters, stateless/read-only modes, byNaturalId). Unwrap when needed.

expert.content:
Optimising, bidirectional relationships, SQL generation and lazy errors

• Optimise slow Hibernate queries: (1) log the SQL and count statements; (2) fix N+1; (3) project only needed columns/DTOs; (4) paginate; (5) add or fix indexes using EXPLAIN ANALYZE; (6) batch writes (sequence ids, batch_size); (7) read-only transactions; (8) cache static data (L2) and measure hit ratio; (9) short transactions and a right-sized pool.
• Bidirectional relationships: choose one owning side (FK), the other mappedBy; keep both in sync via helper methods; avoid collections in equals/hashCode/toString; return DTOs; prefer unidirectional @ManyToOne when you do not need to navigate both ways.
• How Hibernate generates SQL: metadata from annotations builds the mapping model; HQL/JPQL (or Criteria) is parsed into a semantic query model (SQM), translated to the target dialect's SQL AST and rendered as a PreparedStatement; entity operations create actions queued in the ActionQueue and executed at flush through JDBC; results are hydrated into entities and stored in the persistence context.
• Troubleshoot LazyInitializationException: read the stack to see which association and where it is accessed; ensure access happens inside the transaction or fetch it (join fetch/entity graph/DTO); do not fix with EAGER, open-in-view or Hibernate.initialize everywhere; check proxies passing through serialisation (Jackson) and logging.

interviewQA: How do you troubleshoot LazyInitializationException?

Find where the lazy association is accessed outside an open session, then fetch it in the query (join fetch, entity graph) or map to a DTO inside the transaction; avoid switching to EAGER or relying on Open Session In View.
What is the difference between flush() and commit()?

flush writes pending changes to the database within the transaction (still uncommitted and rollback-able); commit flushes and then finalises the transaction, making changes durable and visible to others.
How does Hibernate generate SQL?

It parses HQL/JPQL (or Criteria) into a semantic query model, renders it into dialect-specific SQL as a PreparedStatement, and for entity operations queues actions that are executed at flush through JDBC; results are hydrated into entities tracked by the persistence context.

topics.name: Example: Course, Lesson and Tag Mapping with Fetching and N+1 Fix

beginner.content:
What you build

• A mapped domain: Course 1—* Lesson (parent owns the collection, orphans removed), Course *—* Tag, a query that triggers the N+1 problem and the same query fixed with join fetch.

intermediate.content:
The N+1 problem, seen and fixed

• Listing 50 courses and printing their lessons runs 1 query for courses + 50 queries for lessons. Turn on hibernate.show_sql and count them. The fixes: join fetch, @EntityGraph, or @BatchSize/default_batch_fetch_size.

expert.content:
Checking it in a test

• Assert the number of SQL statements in a test with Hibernate Statistics so a future change cannot reintroduce N+1 silently.

interviewQA: How do you detect and fix N+1 in Hibernate?
Log or count SQL statements, then use join fetch, entity graphs or batch fetching; guard with statistics assertions in tests.
Why keep both sides of a bidirectional association in sync?
Hibernate persists the owning side only; the in-memory graph must be consistent, so use helper methods like addLesson.

topics.name: Example: Optimistic Locking and Retry for Concurrent Updates

beginner.content:
What you build

• Two users edit the same course at the same time. With @Version the second save fails with an OptimisticLockException instead of silently overwriting the first (lost update). A service retries or reports a clear conflict.

intermediate.content: Reproducing the conflict

expert.content:
Retrying and pessimistic alternatives

• For short, idempotent operations retry (Spring Retry @Retryable(retryFor = ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class), outside the transaction). For hot rows or inventory counters use pessimistic locking (@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE), select ... for update) or an atomic update (update stock set qty = qty - 1 where qty > 0). Choose optimistic locking when conflicts are rare.

interviewQA: What problem does @Version solve?
Lost updates: it adds a version check to updates so a stale write fails instead of overwriting newer data.
Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?
Optimistic detects conflicts at commit via a version column and suits rare conflicts; pessimistic locks rows up front and suits high contention.

topics.name: Real-World Scenario: Admin Reports Screen (Projections, Pagination, Bulk Update, Batch Insert)

beginner.content:
The scenario

• An admin screen lists 100,000 enrolments with filters and totals, and a nightly job expires old enrolments. Loading full entities would exhaust memory and trigger N+1 queries. The Hibernate answer: DTO projections, keyset or offset pagination, bulk JPQL updates and JDBC batching.

intermediate.content:
Importing in bulk

• Saving 50,000 entities one by one is slow and fills the persistence context. Use JDBC batching, flush and clear every batch and avoid IDENTITY ids (they disable insert batching): prefer a sequence with allocationSize.

expert.content:
Choosing the right tool

NeedUse
Edit one aggregateEntities + dirty checking
Read-only lists/reportsDTO or interface projections
Update many rows by ruleBulk JPQL/SQL update (bypasses the persistence context: clear it)
Huge importsBatch inserts or JDBC/COPY
Complex analyticsNative SQL / jOOQ / database views
• Watch for pagination with collection fetch (in-memory paging warning) and always add the indexes the filters need.

interviewQA: Why use DTO projections for report screens?
They fetch only needed columns without managed entities, reducing memory and avoiding lazy-loading problems.
Why does IDENTITY prevent insert batching?
The database generates the id on each insert, so Hibernate must execute each insert immediately; sequences let it allocate ids in advance and batch.

cheatNotes: JDBC - Java Database Connectivity, API to connect Java apps to relational DBs
JDBC architecture - Application -> JDBC API -> JDBC Driver -> Database
Type 1 driver - JDBC-ODBC bridge, deprecated, needs ODBC layer
Type 2 driver - Native-API driver, needs vendor DB client library
Type 3 driver - Network protocol driver, uses middleware server
Type 4 driver - Thin/pure Java driver, talks directly to DB (most used)
Class.forName() - Loads and registers the JDBC driver class
DriverManager.getConnection() - Establishes a connection to the database
Connection - Represents an active session with the database
createStatement() - Creates a Statement for static SQL
Statement - Executes plain SQL, vulnerable to SQL injection
PreparedStatement - Precompiled, parameterized query; prevents SQL injection
PreparedStatement is faster for repeated execution of the same query
CallableStatement - Used to execute stored procedures
executeQuery() - Executes SELECT, returns a ResultSet
executeUpdate() - Executes INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, returns affected row count
execute() - Executes any SQL, returns boolean indicating result type
ResultSet - Cursor-based table of query results
ResultSet.next() - Moves cursor to next row, returns false at end
ResultSet types - TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY, TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE, TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE
ResultSetMetaData - Provides info about columns (name, type, count)
DatabaseMetaData - Provides info about the database itself (tables, driver version)
setAutoCommit(false) - Disables auto-commit for manual transaction control
commit() - Permanently saves changes made in the current transaction
rollback() - Reverts changes made since the last commit
Savepoint - Marks an intermediate point for partial rollback
Batch processing - addBatch()/executeBatch() to run multiple statements efficiently
Connection pooling - Reuses DB connections to avoid costly create/close overhead
DataSource - Preferred way to obtain pooled connections (vs DriverManager)
try-with-resources - Auto-closes Connection/Statement/ResultSet to prevent leaks
SQLException - Checked exception thrown on database access errors
getGeneratedKeys() - Retrieves auto-generated keys after an INSERT
RowSet - Lightweight, JavaBean-friendly wrapper around ResultSet
JNDI DataSource - Looks up a connection pool configured on an application server
Statement.setFetchSize() - Controls rows fetched per DB round trip for performance
Isolation levels - READ_UNCOMMITTED, READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE
ORM - Object Relational Mapping, maps Java objects to DB tables
Hibernate - Popular ORM framework implementing JPA specification
JPA vs Hibernate - JPA is a spec, Hibernate is its most popular implementation
SessionFactory - Heavyweight, thread-safe factory that creates Sessions
Session - Lightweight, single-threaded unit of work with the DB
Transaction - Represents a unit of work committed or rolled back atomically
hibernate.cfg.xml - Main configuration file (DB URL, dialect, credentials)
Dialect - Tells Hibernate which SQL flavor to generate for the target DB
@Entity - Marks a class as a persistent entity mapped to a table
@Table - Specifies the table name for an entity
@Id - Marks the primary key field of an entity
@GeneratedValue - Auto-generates primary key values (IDENTITY/SEQUENCE/AUTO/TABLE)
@Column - Maps a field to a specific column, can set name/length/nullable
@OneToOne - Maps a one-to-one relationship between two entities
@OneToMany - Maps a one-to-many relationship (parent to multiple children)
@ManyToOne - Maps many entities referencing a single parent entity
@ManyToMany - Maps a many-to-many relationship via a join table
@JoinColumn - Specifies the foreign key column for a relationship
mappedBy - Marks the inverse (non-owning) side of a bidirectional relationship
session.save() - Inserts a new record and returns generated identifier
session.persist() - Inserts a new record, returns void (JPA-compliant)
session.update() - Reattaches a detached object; throws NonUniqueObjectException only if a DIFFERENT instance with the same id is already in the session
session.merge() - Merges detached object state into a persistent one
session.delete() - Deletes a record from the database
session.get() - Retrieves by ID, returns null if not found (hits DB immediately)
session.load() - Retrieves by ID, returns proxy, throws if not found (lazy)
HQL - Hibernate Query Language, object-oriented, works on entities not tables
Criteria API - Programmatic, type-safe way to build queries (legacy in modern Hibernate)
Native SQL - Hibernate also supports raw SQL queries via createNativeQuery
Transient state - New object not yet associated with a Session
Persistent state - Object associated with an open Session, changes are tracked
Detached state - Object was persistent but its Session is now closed
First-level cache - Session-scoped cache, enabled by default, cannot be disabled
Second-level cache - SessionFactory-scoped cache, shared across sessions, optional
Lazy loading - Associated data fetched only when accessed (default for collections)
Eager loading - Associated data fetched immediately with the parent entity
FetchType.LAZY vs FetchType.EAGER - Controls when related entities are loaded
Cascade - Propagates operations (save/delete/update) from parent to child entities
CascadeType.ALL - Applies all cascade operations to child entities
Optimistic locking - Uses a @Version field to detect concurrent modification conflicts
N+1 problem - Common performance issue from lazy-loading in a loop; fix with JOIN FETCH
Connection pooling - Hibernate integrates with pools like HikariCP for performance
